title: From Security Guard to Rs 50 Lakh a Month: Assam Man's Frozen Paratha Triumph
excerpt: Diganta Das of Gohpur, Assam, went from earning Rs 1,200 a month as a construction labourer to running a frozen Malabar parotta brand that produces over 20,000 parottas a day.
body:
• Diganta Das of Gohpur, Assam, went from earning Rs 1,200 a month as a construction labourer to building DFF (Daily Fresh Food), a frozen Malabar parotta brand that reportedly earns him over Rs 50 lakh a month.
  • After stints as a security guard in Bengaluru and a cook at iD Fresh Food, where he learned to make multi-layered parottas, Das started DFF in 2022 with his entire Rs 7 lakh life savings.
  • The brand now produces more than 20,000 parottas a day and has become one of Assam's leading frozen food businesses.
  • Das's turnaround follows a 2017 accident in which a high-voltage cable left him paralysed for nearly two years — a setback he overcame before launching the venture.

From Rs 1,200 a Month to a Frozen Food Empire

Two decades ago, Diganta Das was a Class 10 graduate earning Rs 1,200 a month as a construction labourer near the Arunachal Pradesh border. Today, the man from Gohpur in Assam's Biswanath district runs DFF (Daily Fresh Food), a frozen Malabar parotta brand that produces more than 20,000 parottas a day and reportedly earns him over Rs 50 lakh every month.

Das's journey, documented by NDTV Food, spans the full arc of India's informal economy: construction worker, hotel room service attendant, security guard, cook — and finally, entrepreneur. The transformation did not come from a lucky break or an investor's backing, but from a skill he picked up on the factory floor and the willingness to stake everything on it.

Context & Background

Growing up in poverty in rural Assam, Das took up work early to support his family. After completing Class 10 in 2001, he joined the Border Roads Organisation as a construction labourer. He later moved to Sikkim for similar work before landing in Bengaluru in 2011, where he worked as a security guard for roughly Rs 4,500 a month and also served as a room service attendant at a hotel. Low wages and delayed payments eventually pushed him out of the job.

The turning point came in 2012, when Das joined iD Fresh Food at Hoskote, Bengaluru, as a cook. Working in large-scale food production, he learned to make multi-layered Malabar parottas and later worked as a dedicated paratha maker. The job gave him something no classroom had: hands-on mastery of a product with genuine commercial demand.

Then came the interruption. In 2017, a high-voltage electric cable fell on him, leaving him paralysed. It took nearly two years to recover. After rehabilitation, an opportunity surfaced: a friend already in the paratha business approached him to help set up a manufacturing unit in Assam. In 2022, Das launched DFF (Daily Fresh Food) with machinery arranged through his friend and his entire life savings — Rs 7 lakh — invested in the venture.

Impact & Analysis

Das began the way most food businesses begin: supplying nearby stores, obsessing over consistent taste and hygiene. Within a year, the soft, crispy parathas had built a loyal base, and DFF expanded across Assam. It now stands as one of the state's leading frozen food brands.

The numbers tell the story of the category itself. India's frozen ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook segment has grown steadily as urban households with less cooking time reach for convenience — and Malabar parotta, a Kerala staple, has travelled far beyond the south. Das's success suggests the category still has room for regional brands that can match national players on taste while beating them on local distribution.

His path also underlines a pattern seen across India's small-business landscape: technical skill acquired on a factory floor, combined with familiarity with a migrant-heavy market like Bengaluru's food industry, translating into an enterprise back home. Das is part of a generation of workers who carried industrial know-how from the metros to their home states — and built businesses with it.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, stories like Das's resonate on two levels. Many diaspora families carry a version of the same arc — parents or grandparents who arrived in new countries with little more than a trade, and built something from it. DFF's frozen parottas also speak to a practical craving: the diaspora market for frozen Indian flatbreads is one of the fastest-growing segments in ethnic grocery, with Malabar parottas a top seller in the US, UK and Gulf. Das's brand is proof that the same product travelling in suitcases and freezer aisles abroad can anchor a Rs 50 lakh-a-month business at home.

What's Next

DFF's next test will be scale: whether the brand can expand beyond Assam while maintaining the quality that built its reputation. Frozen food logistics, cold-chain reliability and competition from national players will decide how far the company can go. Das has said little publicly about expansion plans, but with production already past 20,000 parottas a day, the foundations of a much larger enterprise are in place.
